title: I built a co-op dungeon mode where an LLM runs the table but code holds the dungeon, and the group picks the rules (d20, PbtA, Forged in the Dark…)
author: Medeophoebe
selftext:
Solo dev here. Worldtable is a fantasy RPG where an AI game master runs worlds that people build, and this week I shipped Delves: a quick dungeon run for up to four friends. You pick a dungeon and the rules, make a character in a minute, and send a link. Friends don't need an account. You get what you came for, you get back out, and the run ends in a tale (or an obituary) you can share.

**How the AI is used.** The model writes and judges. Code decides what's true. Each dungeon is a blueprint an LLM designs once from the world's own lore: rooms, doors, keys, seals, traps, who lives there and what they carry, and one goal. A solver then searches it to prove it can be finished before anyone plays it. During play the model narrates and judges whatever you try against notes on how each room works (what the guards can smell, what the beast is afraid of). The outcome tier, its cost, who's standing where and whether a door is actually open all live in the database.

**Any rules.** The host picks the rules for the run: the world's own, or Classic d20, Forged in the Dark, PbtA-style Moves, a couple of d100 systems, or Duality. Code rolls the dice. The model's job is to say which check a move calls for, and the room's outcome follows the roll: a made roll goes clean, a mixed one costs you, a failed one goes badly. The hardest part was getting the judge to stop waving through "I sneak past *very* carefully". A known danger in or next to the room now means you roll, however carefully you do it.

**What broke once friends played together:**

* Hunters were "on you" forever. "On you" meant sharing a zone, so in a long hall the game kept saying they'd caught up while they were 12 squares away. Now it means within reach by the real route.
* An ice wall melted as it went up. How long the wall lasts was also being charged to the dungeon's clock as time spent, so a 15-minute wall's 15 minutes passed the moment it rose.
* One party failed to flee five times in a row. The only exit on a dungeon battle map was the dungeon's own front door, 25 squares off. Now any doorway onto ground the foes don't hold counts as a way out.
* When the leader walked, the others snapped back to their old squares after every step, because the client and the server disagreed about who was following.

**The trailer** was made by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) as a motion piece: HTML and GSAP rendered to video, laid over the game's own map layers, wax seals, painted effects and 3D dice, which were captured frame by frame from the real game. The run itself is scripted: it's a dungeon I wrote for the film, checked and compiled by the real generator.

Every account gets 50 free turns, and guests play on the host's credits. [https://worldtable.gg/worlds?tab=dungeons](https://worldtable.gg/worlds?tab=dungeons&utm_source=reddit&utm_campaign=aigamedev&utm_content=delve)

Curious how others handle this: when an LLM runs a game for several players at once, how do you keep it fair to the person who isn't typing right now?
